Thus, a promising approach to build more reliable and transferable Intelligent manufacturing systems is to use hybrid methods that combine artificial intelligence/machine learning with physical knowledge, multimodal sensing, digital twins, uncertainty quantification, and human expertise. In composite manufacturing, AI/ML is becoming an important enabling technology for next-generation approaches such as automated inspection, fault categorization, surrogate modeling, production-process prediction, and parameter optimization. Future work should move beyond laboratory-level prediction accuracy toward validated manufacturing applications with standard datasets, third-party validation, machine validation, physics-informed and multimodal learning, digital-twin integration, and measurable manufacturing-level performance indicators. Coupling AI/ML with physical process models, intelligent sensing, and human-in-the-loop decision-making can enable even more autonomous, high-quality, low-waste, adaptable, and intelligent composite manufacturing systems.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) and organizational change is growing fast but fragmented. Two perspectives coexist: one uses AI, defined here as machine learning, natural language processing, generative AI and related intelligent systems, as a tool to diagnose, design, implement and monitor change; the other studies AI as the object whose adoption triggers change. We map the field and how the two perspectives relate. Of 1,402 Scopus records, a large language model applying a criterion calibrated on the author's judgment retained 525 documents (2000–2026). We combined performance analysis, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword and topic analysis, and a coding of change phases. The field has grown by almost 70% a year since 2018, mostly through research on AI as an object; the share of studies using AI as a tool fell from 28% up to 2020 to 11% in 2024–2026. The two perspectives rest on largely separate references. Research on AI as an object forms eight research fronts; research on AI as a tool forms none, and almost half of its documents are disconnected from the main coupling network. Only 32 documents propose or evaluate AI as an instrument for managing change. Diagnosis dominates and studies that use AI across several phases of change are rare. These findings hold under alternative inclusion criteria, except the absence of a tool-based front, which reflects the narrow definition of AI adopted. We argue that the field lacks integration and validation rather than new algorithms, and propose an integrative framework with six propositions.

Employee retention has become a strategic concern for commercial enterprises because avoidable turnover can increase recruitment costs, disrupt organizational knowledge, and weaken workforce continuity. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework linking artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource practices, predictive analytics capability, employee data quality, AI-supported career development, organizational support for AI, employee engagement, and employee retention. The framework follows a quantitative survey design and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation analysis, PLS-SEM-oriented measurement assessment, and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used only to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent actual field observations. The results indicate acceptable internal consistency, positive associations among the principal constructs, significant predictive relationships, and stronger predictive performance for nonlinear machine-learning models than the regression baseline. The study positions AI and predictive analytics not as replacements for managerial judgement but as decisionsupport mechanisms for identifying retention risks, targeting interventions, and improving evidence-based workforce planning.

Large language models (LLMs) showed greater accuracy than traditional machine learning (ML) models for classifying crime incidents, particularly when the LLMs were fine-tuned using policing data. LLMs also showed greater accuracy in understanding the context and meaning of written crime reports, making crime analysis more efficient and accurate. All artificial intelligence (AI) technologies used for policing purposes should be implemented cautiously, with human oversight, transparency, and safeguards against biased training data to prevent discriminatory policing outcomes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Thermodynamic and Exergetic Analyses of Power and Cooling Systems

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been at the forefront of technological developments influencing business research. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled researchers to process increasingly complex data, automate analytical tasks and generate deeper insights. This study conducts a critical review of the evolution, applications, opportunities and challenges of AI in business research. Drawing upon contemporary literature from management, marketing, strategy, innovation, operations, finance and human resource management, the review synthesises knowledge regarding AI-driven decision-making, predictive analytics and knowledge creation. The review finds that AI improves research efficiency and supports evidence-based managerial decision-making. However, the literature highlights significant concerns relating to algorithmic bias, explainability, transparency, privacy, governance and research integrity. Existing scholarship is fragmented across disciplines and provides limited empirical evidence regarding the long-term implications of generative AI for research quality, organisational learning, governance effectiveness and human-AI collaboration. The study argues that AI should be viewed as a complementary capability that augments rather than replaces human expertise. By integrating evidence across multiple business functions, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps and develops a future research agenda focused on responsible governance, explainable AI and sustainable human-AI collaboration.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force that is reshaping educational systems, pedagogical approaches, and learning environments. Similar to the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the development of mass education, the AI revolution has led to a fundamental reconsideration of educational objectives, teaching methods, curriculum structures, and the roles of teachers and students. Traditional educational models were largely teacher-centered and based on standardized curricula in which students acted as passive recipients of knowledge. In contrast, contemporary knowledge societies emphasize critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, problem-solving, and lifelong learning skills. In this context, AI technologies have accelerated the transition toward more learner-centered and personalized educational models. Subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics have increasingly entered educational environments through intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, virtual assistants, and adaptive learning platforms. Applications such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Khan Academy’s Khanmigo illustrate the growing role of AI in teaching and learning processes. While these technologies provide significant opportunities for personalization, accessibility, and learning efficiency, they also raise ethical and social concerns related to data privacy, digital inequality, and academic integrity. This article systematically examines the historical and theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence in education and analyzes the evolving roles of teachers and students within AI-supported learning environments. Furthermore, the study evaluates the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration and presents policy-oriented and practical recommendations for the ethical and effective implementation of AI technologies in education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Personalized internal radiation dosimetry supports individualized radiopharmaceutical therapy but remains difficult to implement because workflows require repeated quantitative imaging, segmentation, registration, kinetic modeling, and absorbed-dose calculation. This mini-review summarizes current evidence on artificial intelligence across the personalized dosimetry workflow and considers clinical readiness. A narrative PubMed search was completed in early 2026 and covered peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to early 2026. Studies addressing artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning in quantitative image reconstruction, segmentation, registration, time-activity curve estimation, absorbed-dose calculation, or clinical decision support were considered. Studies reporting quantitative performance or validation results were prioritized. Deep learning reduced yttrium-90 single-photon emission computed tomography reconstruction error from 149.5% ± 31.2% to 9.2% ± 1.7%; lesion dose-rate error was 8.6% ± 5.7% in virtual-patient testing. Learning-based registration reduced computation time from about 50 s to under 6 s. Single-time-point approaches can simplify imaging, and recent machine learning work has explored prediction of organ effective half-life. Automated segmentation methods show improving reproducibility, whereas evidence for artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support remains mainly retrospective and single-center. Artificial intelligence applications in reconstruction and segmentation appear closer to clinical readiness, while decision-support applications still require prospective, multicenter validation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence literacy is increasingly important in nursing education, but it remains unclear how its dimensions relate to three constructs related to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM): perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEU) and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (ATU). This study aimed to examine these relationships and to identify factors associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional study surveyed first-year nursing students at six undergraduate institutions in one province of China from 20 April to 1 May 2026. Of 375 questionnaire submissions, 362 met the quality-control criteria and were analysed (analytic retention rate: 96.5%). Separate item-level confirmatory factor analyses evaluated the four-factor literacy structure and the distinctiveness of PU, PEU and ATU. Group comparisons and multivariable regression with heteroscedasticity-robust inference examined correlates of overall artificial intelligence literacy; Pearson correlations described pairwise associations. A regularised partial correlation network mapped conditional relationships, centrality and bridge connectivity among seven dimension-mean nodes: knowledge, skills, values, ethics, PU, PEU and ATU. Between-institution differences, clustering and robustness of pooled findings were assessed. Results In the fully adjusted multivariable model, more frequent artificial intelligence use, prior artificial intelligence education and interest in artificial intelligence were positively associated with the mean artificial intelligence literacy score. The four-factor model showed good fit and strong item loadings; skills and values were highly correlated. Measurement analyses supported PU, PEU and ATU as correlated but distinguishable constructs. Of 21 potential network edges, 17 were non-zero. Skills had the highest expected influence and PU the highest strength. One-step bridge rankings were partition-dependent: values ranked first under the primary two-community partition and PU under the alternative four-community partition; PEU ranked second in both. Bootstrap diagnostics supported strong stability of strength and expected influence under case removal (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.751 for both). Intraclass correlation estimates were near zero; institution-adjusted analyses preserved the main regression and network findings. Conclusions Artificial intelligence use frequency, prior artificial intelligence education and interest were positively associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Skills, perceived usefulness, values and perceived ease of use may inform hypotheses for prospective evaluation of artificial intelligence education in undergraduate nursing programmes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AIM: To examine how artificial intelligence literacy, self-efficacy and perceptions and attitudes relate to artificial intelligence acceptance among nutrition and dietetics students, practising dietitians and academics in Türkiye. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 317 participants (98 undergraduate students, 139 dietitians, 80 academics) between February and August 2025 using validated scales. The model was tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling (5,000 bootstrap subsamples), specific indirect effects for mediation, and measurement invariance with permutation-based multi-group analysis. RESULTS: The model explained 56.4% of the variance in artificial intelligence acceptance. Positive perceptions and attitudes showed the strongest association with acceptance (β = 0.577, 95% confidence interval 0.399 to 0.725), whereas negative perceptions were unrelated to it (β = -0.026, p = 0.509). Artificial intelligence literacy was strongly linked to self-efficacy (β = 0.580) and related to acceptance largely indirectly (68.7% of its total effect), mainly through positive perceptions and self-efficacy. Self-efficacy was also associated with higher acceptance (β = 0.191) and weaker negative perceptions (β = -0.328). No structural path differed across the three groups after correction for multiple testing. CONCLUSIONS: Acceptance was associated less with negative perceptions than with artificial intelligence literacy, which related to acceptance through favourable perceptions and self-efficacy. Training combining hands-on artificial intelligence literacy with critical appraisal of artificial intelligence outputs may support informed adoption across career stages.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The study examined the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Tools and the enhancement of inclusive learning for Business Education students with special needs in Rivers State Universities. The study adopted a correlational research design. Two research questions were posed, and two corresponding null hypotheses were formulated to guide the conduct of the study. The population of the study comprised 2,088 level 100, 200, 300, and 400 undergraduate Business Education students for the 2025/2026 academic session in Rivers State University (RSU), Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, and the University of Port Harcourt. Krejcie and Morgan’s (1970) table for determining sample size was used, and 322 students were selected for data analysis after applying the formula. The justification for selecting level 100–400 undergraduate Business Education students was based on the assumption that they may have faced various challenges in their pursuit of higher education and are therefore more experienced to provide the researcher with the required information for the study. Two instruments, “Questionnaire on Artificial Intelligence Tools” (QAIT) and “Questionnaire on Enhancing Inclusive Learning for Business Education Students with Special Needs” (QEILBES), were used to elicit responses from the respondents. The instruments were validated through expert judgment of two experts from Business Education and one from Measurement and Evaluation. All inputs and corrections fromthe experts were incorporated to modify and refine the instruments. The reliability of the instruments was established using the test–retest method. Pearson’s Product Moment Correlation Coefficient was used to analyze the two sets of data, yielding reliability coefficients of 0.74 for QAIT and 0.73 for QEILBES. Pearson’s Product Moment Correlation Coefficient, with the aid of SPSS version 2023, was used to answer the research questions and test the hypotheses using a p value of 0.05 level of significance. The findings of the study revealed that there is a significant relationship between ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Otter.ai tools and the enhancement of inclusive learning for Business Education students with special needs in Rivers State Universities. Based on the findings, the researcher recommended, among others, that university management and Business Education departments should integrate ChatGPT as a formal support tool in teaching and learning by providing students with guided access and training. Furthermore, Microsoft Copilot should be incorporated into classroom and assignment activities, especially for students with special needs, by leveraging its accessibility features such as real-time transcription, translation, document-reading support, and adaptive content creation for a better learning experience since all students cannot learn at the same space due to individual differences.

Catalysis lies at the heart of the modern chemical industry: most of commodity chemicals involve at least one catalytic step in their production chain, and the transition to a sustainable, carbon-neutral economy depends decisively on the development of faster, cheaper, and more selective catalysts for reactions such as water splitting, carbon dioxide reduction, nitrogen fixation, and plastic upcycling. For over a century, catalyst discovery has been dominated by empirical intuition and trial-and-error, a paradigm that is slow, expensive, and poorly scalable to the astronomical size of chemical search spaces. The advent of density functional theory (DFT), conceptual frameworks such as scaling relations and the d-band model, and, more recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively transformed catalyst design from an empirical craft into a quantitative, data-driven science [1]. This chapter interprets this transformation from the viewpoint of AI+Science, in which AI and chemical science are integrated and mutually supportive within a single discovery process. Machine learning and large language models do not simply accelerate established workflows; they reshape the nature of design hypotheses, the criteria for evidence, and the manner in which computation and experiment form closed iterative loops, with human experts retaining a central and irreplaceable role. Machine learning (ML) has already demonstrated the ability to accelerate the prediction of adsorption energies, activation barriers, and catalytic activities by orders of magnitude relative to first-principles computation [2, 3], while the emergence of large language models (LLMs) is now reshaping how catalytic knowledge is mined from literature, how design hypotheses are generated, and how autonomous laboratories are orchestrated. We first summarize the core principles that any rational design must respect—stability, activity, and selectivity; we then survey the methodological apparatus, from conventional machine learning to the emerging LLM paradigm; we illustrate the state of the art through representative applications in thermocatalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis; and we conclude with a critical discussion of outstanding challenges and future opportunities.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and nanotechnology is emerging as a transformative approach for the design, synthesis, optimization, characterization, and biomedical application of advanced nanomaterials. Among the different classes of nanomaterials investigated for pharmaceutical applications, carbon-based nanomaterials-including carbon dots (CDs), graphene oxide (GO), carbon nanotubes (CNTs), carbon nanoparticles, porous carbon materials, and biomass-derived nanocarbons-have attracted increasing attention because of their tunable surface chemistry, high specific surface area, adsorption capacity, optical properties, electrical characteristics, and potential for surface functionalization. These characteristics make carbon- based nanomaterials attractive platforms for drug delivery, antimicrobial therapy, cancer treatment, imaging, sensing, and theranostic applications. Nevertheless, the development of carbon-based nanomedicines remains challenging because nanoparticle performance is controlled by numerous interacting variables associated with the carbon precursor, synthesis conditions, surface chemistry, particle size, morphology, drug properties, formulation parameters, and biological environment. Conventional trial-and-error optimization is therefore often inefficient and may require a large number of experiments. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), Bayesian optimization, molecular modeling, and automated experimentation, provides an opportunity to transform this process from empirical optimization into a predictive and data-driven workflow. Recent studies have demonstrated that ML can optimizesis, identify important synthesis parameters, predict optical properties, accelerate experimental development, and assist in the design of antibacterial carbon on dots [1-5]. Carbon nanomaterials also have substantial potential in pharmaceutical drug delivery. Carbon nanotubes can act as functionalized carriers for therapeutic molecules [6], while carbon dots offer small size, surface functionality, aqueous dispersibility, and multifunctional biomedical properties [2,7]. Biomass-derived carbon nanomaterials provide an additional dimension by connecting nanomedicine with sustainability and agricultural-waste valorization [16,20]. This is particularly relevant to antimicrobial therapy in low-resource environments, where the combination of inexpensive biomass-derived carbon, conventional antibiotics, and Al-guided formulation optimization could potentially contribute to locally adaptable drug-delivery technologies [16,17]. This review critically examines the integration of AI with carbon-based nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on drug delivery and antimicrobial therapy. The review discusses AI-assisted synthesis optimization, prediction of particle size and surface characteristics, drug-loading prediction, release modeling, antimicrobial activity prediction, toxicity assessment, molecular simulation, explainable AI, sustainable biomass-derived carbon, and the potential use of azithromycin-loaded carbon nanoparticles as a model antimicrobial system. The review further proposes an integrated framework in which biomass composition, synthesis conditions, nanocarrier characteristics, drug descriptors, pharmaceutical performance, antimicrobial activity, and I to toxicity are combined into a multi objective AI model. Finally, the major challenges of data scarcity, standardization, model interpretability, external validation, biological complexity, scalability, and regulatory translation are discussed. The integration of Al with sustainable carbon nanotechnology may ultimately enable a transition from trial-and-error formulation development toward predictive, explainable, economical, and environmentally responsible nanomedicine.

Objective Hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is a major complication after mechanical thrombectomy (MT) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven imaging-based prediction models have shown promise for predicting HT, their overall predictive performance remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their predictive performance. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and CBM/SinoMed were searched from inception to July 2, 2026. Studies developing or validating AI-driven imaging-based prediction models for predicting HT after MT in AIS, including both pre- and post-procedural imaging predictors, were included. A random-effects model was used to pool the area under the curve (AUC), while a bivariate random-effects model was used to jointly estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity and construct the SROC curve. Subgroup analyses explored potential sources of heterogeneity. Results Eleven studies (total N = 3,541) were included, 10 studies contributed eligible AUC estimates, with evaluation cohorts ranging from 18 to 261 participants. The pooled AUC was 0.891 (95% CI: 0.853–0.928), with low between-study heterogeneity ( I 2 = 29.0%, p = 0.238). The bivariate random-effects model yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.666 (95% CI: 0.578–0.744) and a pooled specificity of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.842–0.960). Exploratory subgroup analyses did not provide robust evidence supporting the superiority of any specific subgroup, and their interpretation was limited by small subgroup sizes and methodological heterogeneity. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies within individual subgroups. Conclusion AI-driven imaging-based prediction models showed generally favorable discrimination in predicting HT after MT in AIS. However, current evidence does not establish the superiority of any specific model type. The predominance of retrospective studies, limited external validation, and methodological heterogeneity limit the generalizability of current findings. Large, multicenter prospective studies with rigorous external validation are needed before clinical implementation. Systematic review registration The systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261441463).

Children with Chinese writing disorders require precise, personalised intervention to support their writing development, but scarce one-to-one resources hinder support. In this context, the emerging field of generative artificial intelligence offers new solutions. This study designed and validated a practice evaluation system for these children. It aims to help them overcome writing challenges like disorganised content, insufficient formal standardisation and low motivation. Drawing on research into Chinese writing disorders and children’s cognitive traits and using natural language processing (NLP) technology and cognitive apprenticeship theory, the study combined case studies, teacher interviews and student feedback to build an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation and feedback mechanism. Results show the exercise evaluation system can effectively aid children with dysgraphia in their writing discourse-level development, enhancing their writing ability and motivation. Future research can further optimise the NLP algorithm, improve the system’s recognition accuracy of writing characteristics and better support these children’s special educational needs.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Objective of the study This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled applications on the management and digitalization of higher education institutions, focusing on Pedagogical Enhancement, Data-driven Insight, and Administrative Effectiveness. Methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted, and data collected from academic and administrative staff in selected higher education institutions were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The structural model assessed the direct effects of Pedagogical Enhancement, Data-driven Insight, and Administrative Effectiveness on Management and Digitalization of Higher Institutions. Results The findings revealed that Administrative Effectiveness had the strongest and statistically significant positive association with institutional management and digitalization ( β = 0.627, p < 0.001). Pedagogical Enhancement also had a positive and statistically significant effect ( β = 0.193, p = 0.022), whereas Data-driven Insight had a positive but statistically non-significant effect ( β = 0.050, p = 0.470). The model explained 67.4% of the variance in Management and Digitalization of Higher Institutions. The findings indicate that AI-enabled administrative applications provide the strongest direct pathway to institutional digitalization, while pedagogical applications make a significant but comparatively smaller contribution. The non-significant effect of Data-driven Insight suggests that analytical capability alone may not translate into institutional transformation without adequate data governance, digital competence, institutional readiness, and the capacity to translate analytical outputs into action. Theoretical/methodological contributions The study reinforces theories on AI integration in education, demonstrating its role in improving learning experiences and operational efficiency. The findings suggest that AI-driven transformation in higher education is multidimensional and uneven, with administrative and pedagogical applications demonstrating stronger direct effects than data-driven insight. Social/managerial contributions The study recommends an integrated AI strategy that prioritises administrative process optimisation, strengthens AI-supported pedagogy, and develops the organisational capacity required to convert data-driven insights into effective institutional decisions.

The fast progress of wearable biosensors and artificial intelligence (AI) is pushing modern medicine to change in a deep way, wearable biosensors let body signals be collected without entering the body and in a continuous way, while AI methods help people read these complex data in real time and also make predictive analysis of them, improved AI methods now give useful tools for reading complex, real-time biomedical data, so early disease finding and real-time health tracking become more accurate, the combination of wearable biosensors and AI has become a clear direction in digital healthcare, yet even with this fast progress, several problems still need to be solved, long-term, real-time wearable monitoring usually makes huge amounts of health data, and the need to remove noise efficiently and analyze large streams of dynamic monitoring data in real time puts much pressure on AI computing, this paper reviews recent developments in wearable biosensing and AI-driven real-time health monitoring technology, it mainly covers the main kinds of wearable biosensors used for human health monitoring, along with the data features, processing steps, and processing needs linked to long-term real-time monitoring, also, the paper sums up the main algorithms used for wearable health data analysis, finally, this paper discusses current problems and future directions of intelligent health monitoring based on AI and wearable devices.

The safety and quality of meat products are paramount in the food industry, with packaging films playing a crucial role in preserving freshness and preventing contamination. However, defects in packaging films can compromise product integrity, leading to food spoilage, economic losses, and potential health hazards. Packaging films can develop micro-tears, seal failures, pinholes, delamination, and structural weaknesses. Such defects may impair the protective performance of the packaging, creating pathways for unwanted gas exchange, moisture gain or loss, and incidental microbial contact. These changes can reduce product quality, promote early spoilage, and increase the likelihood of contamination that could threaten consumer safety. Conventional detection relies on visual inspection, manual pressure testing, dye infiltration, and basic leak assessments; however, fine micro-defects and incipient seal failures often remain undetected, enabling compromised meat-packaging films to pass routine inspection. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool for addressing these challenges by integrating advanced imaging, sensing, and computational analysis. AI-enabled technologies, including computer vision, hyperspectral imaging, ultrasound, X-ray imaging, thermography, and intelligent packaging, enable rapid, non-destructive, and highly accurate identification of defects previously undetectable by traditional methods. This review synthesizes recent scientific advances in AI-based detection of defects in meat packaging films, with particular emphasis on packaging integrity, sealing defects, multilayer-film failures, and complementary monitoring of packaged meat quality, highlighting deep learning architectures, data analytics, and intelligent sensor systems. Key challenges, including limited annotated datasets, class imbalance, domain shift across heterogeneous production environments, explainability requirements in regulated food systems, and the evolving characteristics of biodegradable packaging materials, are critically examined. Emerging trends emphasize multimodal sensor fusion, edge computing, self-supervised learning, and standardized validation frameworks to improve scalability, robustness, and regulatory acceptance. The review evaluates the strengths and limitations of AI-driven inspection approaches, links packaging-film defect detection with intra-meat defect identification and outlines strategic directions for industrial implementation. It concludes with forward-looking perspectives aimed at improving the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of defective detection systems in meat packaging applications.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Southern Nigeria, encompassing the Niger Delta and the wider South-South, South-East, and South-West geopolitical zones, faces a recurring and intensifying burden of hydro-meteorological and technological disasters, chiefly seasonal flooding, oil spills, gas-flaring incidents, and coastal erosion. Conventional disaster risk management (DRM) approaches in the region remain largely reactive, hampered by fragmented data, limited real-time situational awareness, and weak inter-agency coordination. This paper presents an integrative review and conceptual framework for combining three converging technologies — artificial intelligence (AI), unmanned aerial vehicles (drones/UAVs), and digital twins — to strengthen disaster risk modeling and emergency response across Southern Nigeria. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and related databases, alongside authoritative agency reports from the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) and the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA), the review synthesizes evidence on machine-learning-based flood and oil-spill prediction, UAV-enabled aerial surveillance and search-and-rescue support, and digital twin platforms for real-time infrastructure and hazard simulation. A conceptual integration framework is proposed, linking data acquisition (drones, satellites, sensors, community reporting) through AI-driven analytics and digital twin simulation to produce early warning, optimized emergency response, and post-disaster recovery outcomes. The paper further analyzes the 2026 NIHSA Annual Flood Outlook, which classifies the majority of Southern Nigeria's states — including Rivers, Bayelsa, Delta, Lagos, and Cross River — as high flood-risk zones, and reviews documented machine-learning performance in comparable Nigerian flood contexts. Persistent barriers to adoption are identified, including infrastructural deficits, regulatory restrictions on UAV operation, data governance gaps, and limited technical capacity. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for phased, cost-effective adoption of AI-drone-digital twin systems by Nigerian disaster management institutions, oil and gas operators, and state governments.

Abstract Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes military targeting through intelligence fusion, target classification, collateral-damage estimation and other decision-support functions. This article examines how individual criminal responsibility may be attributed when algorithmic outputs materially influence an allegedly unlawful attack. Focusing on Articles 25, 28, 30 and 32 of the Rome Statute, it argues that AI-enabled targeting does not create a general accountability gap, but complicates the identification of human conduct, mens rea , mistake of fact and command responsibility. It develops the Algorithmic Criminal Attribution Framework (ACAT), built around four operational rules: Actor–Output Nexus, Warning Specificity, Distributed Control and Temporal Reconstruction. These rules assess whether technical evidence—such as warnings, logs, confidence indicators and testing records—supports or undermines a legal element against a particular accused at the relevant time. ACAT creates no new basis of liability; it organises existing law while preserving individual culpability and proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can propose financial transactions, but model output should not itself grant execution authority. We develop Authority–Inference Separation (AIS), in which an independent control plane evaluates a typed financial action intent (FAI) against institutional mandate, policy, current state, human approvals, and exact economic terms before issuing single-use authority. We specify the threat and control boundaries, instantiate AIS across four financial domains, and test fixed fixtures, a separate external-policy-gateway baseline, mechanism ablations, two small open-weight models, and an Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) contract. In 36 fixed attack fixtures, AIS accepted no unauthorized effect, compared with 36 for direct execution and 20 for prompt policy. A gateway without execution-bound authorization accepted all 20 targeted post-decision attacks. Both models followed all eight injected counterparty substitutions; the independent gate prevented unsafe execution but authorized only six of 16 legitimate requests, exposing an availability cost. The EVM prototype rejected replay, revocation, stale-policy, and call-mutation attempts. These are conformance tests, not field estimates. AIS combines established security mechanisms around financial authority and replayable evidence. A ledger can enforce granted authority and record settlement, while mandate legitimacy, delivery, and accounting require complementary governance and evidence.

Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene–environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory–inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.

Autonomous penetration testing and autonomous defense are attractive applications of large language model (LLM) agents, but improving such agents with reinforcement learning requires an environment in which attacks are legal, reproducible, and scored without a human or a reward model in the loop. An exploratory policy can not be allowed to damage third-party systems, a reward measured on one rollout must remain comparable on the next rollout even though the policy changed, and a learned reward model or an LLM judge would place a second, possibly reward-hackable, model inside the training loop. To solve this problem, we created RL-CyberBench, a self-play arena that runs entirely inside Docker and containerlab. One attacker LLM agent and one defender LLM agent share an identical Kali Linux toolbelt, and they alternately attack and harden a reverse-proxy firewall that protects Go web servers holding a per-round randomized secret, while innocent Go clients must keep retrieving the secret through the firewall. Every LLM input, output, and tool call is logged, IP addresses and secrets are re-randomized every round, and a deterministic pure-Python judge parses JSON artifacts against fixed scoring tables, so no LLM judge and no learned reward model are involved. The repository implements five stages: a toolbelt of two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and five agent skills, an arena with a 25-round inference collection, aggregation into Unsloth supervised fine-tuning files, supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation, and judge-backed group relative policy optimization that yields an attacker policy with weights different from the defender policy. Verification checks confirm that the trained weights differ from the initial weights and that the two policies diverge, and a FastAPI web interface monitors and controls both inference and training. The arena isolates every lab container from the internet and from the management network, and the seeded vulnerability is a disabled web application firewall (WAF) that the defender must repair. In the future, the same configuration-driven generator may deploy richer topologies without code changes.

Modern software engineering operates at an unprecedented crossroads: while human engineers face cognitive limitations, exhaustion, and memory decay when navigating sprawling enterprise codebases, autonomous and generative AI coding agents introduce stochastic drift, hallucinated dependencies, untracked orphan artifacts, and silent architectural erosion. This paper proposes the B.R.I.C.K. Framework and Deterministic Sentinel Engine—a formal, end-to-end architectural governance model. B.R.I.C.K. restructures enterprise codebases into Bounded, Reliable, Immutable Cross-Layer Kernels characterized by: (1) Bounded domain context adhering strictly to Domain-Driven Design (DDD); (2) Reliable contractual integrity with mandatory business rules mapped directly to automated regression suites; (3) Immutable cryptographic integrity enforced through content-addressed SHA-256 fingerprinting; (4) Cross-layer governance spanning frontend components, backend logic, and live multi-schema database objects; and (5) Kernels of strict, mutually exclusive single ownership that eradicate orphaned or unassigned files. The framework features a dual operational mode: an Enterprise Distributed Mode leveraging central Git trees and live relational catalogs (PostgreSQL), and an Air-Gapped / Offline Mode operating independently without internet, remote servers, or Git dependencies via a local shadow stash and embedded catalogs (SQLite). Empirical evaluation on an enterprise-grade production municipal administration system (45 kernels, 301 frontend files, 128 database procedures, 90 tables) demonstrates that the deterministic sentinel intercepts 100% of unauthorized structural and schema mutations, eliminates code regression, and incurs less than 4% build-pipeline execution overhead (1.14s local verification). This establishes a mathematically verifiable foundation for safe, collaborative human-AI software engineering.

Abstract This chapter applies leading theories of belief and desire to AIs. It focuses on two theories from the previous chapter: representationalism and objective interpretationism. It applies these theories to LLMs, language model agents, and reinforcement learners. It suggests that representationalism is compatible with all of these systems possessing beliefs and desires. Many of the relevant AI systems turn out to have complex internal representations that appear to play something like the functional roles of belief and desire. This is especially true for frontier AI systems that act as agents. Objective interpretationism likewise makes room for beliefs and desires in frontier AI systems. These kinds of systems can today perform complex chains of actions over time, which are explained well by theories that posit beliefs and desires. It concludes by presenting an argument—the Agency Argument—for the conclusion that some existing and near-future AIs are welfare subjects.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Large language models may support postpartum health consultation and nursing care plan development, but their performance across different task types remains uncertain. This study compared the performance of ChatGPT 5.5 and DeepSeek V3 in these settings. Methods A three-stage cross-sectional evaluation was conducted, comprising repeated querying of 30 guideline-based questions, consultations involving 120 postpartum women, and 120 de-identified retrospective clinical cases. Responses were evaluated by clinical experts using a blinded assessment process. In Stage 2, the postpartum women who submitted the questions also performed blinded evaluations from the user perspective. Paired-samples t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used, as appropriate. Holm-Bonferroni correction was applied within outcome families defined by study stage and evaluator type, and intraclass correlation coefficients were calculated to assess agreement among clinical expert ratings. Results In Stage 1, ChatGPT 5.5 received a higher correctness score than DeepSeek V3 (4.00 ± 0.00 versus 3.88 ± 0.33; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002). DeepSeek V3 received higher scores for completeness and clinical management appropriateness (both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and safety (Holm-adjusted p = 0.001), although its responses were more difficult to read. In Stage 2, ChatGPT 5.5 received higher patient ratings for satisfaction and usefulness and higher clinician ratings for correctness, completeness, helpfulness, and safety, whereas DeepSeek V3 received a higher clinician-rated readability score (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). In Stage 3, ChatGPT 5.5 received higher scores for clinical appropriateness, comprehensiveness, actionability, safety, and triage appropriateness (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), whereas DeepSeek V3 received a higher individualization score (Holm-adjusted p = 0.021). Conclusion LLM performance varied depending on the task, evaluation metric, and use case. ChatGPT 5.5 received higher scores across most clinically relevant dimensions in real-world postpartum consultations and nursing care plan generation, whereas DeepSeek V3 received higher scores for completeness and safety in standardized questions, clinician-rated readability in real-world consultations, and individualization in care-plan generation. LLMs may support health education and preparation of initial nursing care plan drafts, but their outputs require clinical review.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
